extracted.intended_audience: design patent applicants, patent practitioners, and IP litigators (including law students and examiners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to draft and present drawings and related wording in U.S. design patent applications so that the claim scope is definite, enforceable, and appropriately tied to an article of manufacture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include an article of manufacture (35 U.S.C. § 171 requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A design patent must apply a shape, configuration, or surface ornamentation to a specific article of manufacture; a patent cannot claim a pattern 'in the abstract' without reference to an article of manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference Curver Luxembourg v. Home Expressions: drawings that depict only a pattern without a specific article led to the Federal Circuit construing the patent as limited to chairs (the referenced article) and rejecting attempts to cover every possible article. Ensure the drawings and title/claim link the design to a concrete article of manufacture to avoid being limited or invalidated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not claim surface ornamentation in the abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patents should not be drafted so as to attempt to protect a surface ornamentation per se across every possible article of manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court has stated it 'has never sanctioned granting a design patent for a surface ornamentation in the abstract such that the patent's scope encompasses every possible article of manufacture to which the surface ornamentation is applied.' Avoid claiming a pattern alone without tying it to particular article(s) or clear claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use wording/title and drawings together to define the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the invention in the words and title as well as in the drawings; relying on 'abstracted' drawings without corresponding descriptive wording risks rejection or litigation defeat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curver demonstrates that disassociated drawings and indefinite wording can lead to a patent being construed narrowly or invalidated. Include clear title/claim language that identifies the article of manufacture and harmonizes with the figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual disclosure must not be internally inconsistent
rubrics_metrics.description: A visual disclosure may be inadequate—and its associated claim indefinite—if it includes multiple, internally inconsistent drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit in In re Maatita noted that inconsistencies in drawings can render a claim indefinite, but inconsistencies do not merit § 112 rejection if they 'do not preclude the overall understanding of the drawing as a whole.' Ensure multiple figures are consistent or collectively convey a clear, unified design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meet the definiteness standard: inform with reasonable certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim, read in light of the visual disclosure, must 'inform, with reasonable certainty, those skilled in the art about the scope of the invention.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Nautilus and In re Maatita, the key test is whether the disclosure gives potential competitors notice of what design is claimed. Draft drawings and text so that an ordinary observer and those skilled in the art can reasonably ascertain claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary observer test allows multiple embodiments if scope is clear
rubrics_metrics.description: A single design patent drawing may disclose multiple embodiments and still be definite if the scope is clear with reasonable certainty to an ordinary observer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Maatita upheld that a two-dimensional drawing of a three-dimensional sole could be definite even if multiple 3D realizations are possible, provided an ordinary observer understands the claimed two-dimensional aspect. Use drawings that convey the aspect of the design that would be perceived by the ordinary observer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of detail should match whether the design is definable by a planar illustration
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of drawing detail required depends on whether the claimed design for the article can be defined by a two-dimensional, plan- or planar-view illustration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the design is typically considered in a planar view (e.g., rug, shoe sole), a 2D drawing may suffice; for designs requiring depth/contour clarity, include additional views or detail to avoid indefiniteness or enablement objections. Evaluate whether additional perspectives are necessary to convey the claimed design unambiguously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid leaving design open to multiple patentably-distinct interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: If a drawing allows multiple plausible three-dimensional implementations that would be patentably distinct, an examiner may find the claim indefinite or not enabled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Maatita the examiner produced four different 3D renderings from a single 2D figure and concluded they were patentably distinct. Anticipate such alternate interpretations and either refine the drawings/text to narrow the intended scope or add figures/description to show the intended embodiment(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategically choose drawings and wording to control claim breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: The right drawing and accompanying wording can broaden the scope of a design patent; the wrong drawing/wording can destroy or unduly limit it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use claims, title, and figures intentionally to capture desired scope. Consider whether to allow multiple interpretations (to broaden) or expressly limit embodiments (to avoid indefiniteness). Be mindful that overly abstract figures risk rejection or narrow construction in litigation, while well-chosen figures can cover multiple embodiments when appropriate.
